tldr: Dubois built Boot UI, a Spring Boot developer console, in 11 days through 223 agent-written pull requests, and shares six ingredients: model choice, specs, tests, tools, parallelism, overnight runs.
summary: Dubois, creator of JHipster and now at GitHub, built an open-source project so he could show real numbers: Boot UI, a developer console for Spring Boot (Spring, Hibernate, a Vue.js front end) he had estimated at over six months of solo work. Time-boxed to 11 days of normal hours, it reached 1.0.0 with 223 merged pull requests, about 20 a day, mostly committed by Copilot agents in parallel, with unusually large amounts of specs and tests. He puts the gain at 15 to 20 times, for about $2,000 in tokens. The project has since passed 500 PRs, 20 releases and nearly 400,000 lines without a maintenance tax.

His ingredients: stick with one main model, partly to keep the 90% cached-token discount, have other models "rubber duck" complex work (half his tokens), and use small models for speed. Write specs: an AGENTS.md pinning Maven, JUnit, Docker Compose and Spotless so parallel agents stay consistent, plus specs defining done. Write tests: agents loop locally, then on GitHub Actions with CodeQL, fixing failed PRs themselves. Specs and tests form the harness, which he says matters more than the model. Equip agents: the Impeccable UI skill, Copilot's agent-merge (he never resolved a conflict by hand), a custom release skill, and the Eclipse JDT language server, saving about 20% of tokens.

The human ingredients: run many independent tasks in parallel and act as the manager of a fleet, and restructure the day. From 11:00 he orchestrates normal tasks, around 17:00 he writes specs for two or three big tasks to run overnight, and from 9:00 to 11:00 he reviews and merges their results. Caveats: Boot UI's panels are repetitive and Spring is well documented, so expect perhaps 10x elsewhere; beware scope creep, too many large PRs and underpowered models. GitHub issues and PR comments act as specs, and the Copilot mobile app and cloud agent (one-hour limit) take experiments off his laptop.

On token economics, a quiz showed that 2,000 output tokens cost more than 100,000 cached input tokens, and that switching to a half-price model can cost more because it busts the cache, as do editing AGENTS.md, compacting history or a five-minute coffee break. Caching saves only about 51% overall because output is uncached. Copilot's auto mode gives a 10% discount and is cache-aware, and a research-preview Fusion mode cascades and cross-checks models. He ended by starting a release preparation from his own agent and skill in the Copilot app, and noted that Boot UI is itself an MCP server and skill.
keyPoints: Boot UI 1.0.0: 223 merged PRs in 11 working days, versus his estimate of more than six months by hand, at roughly $2,000 in tokens.
Half of his tokens go to rubber ducking, where other models audit what the main model produced.
The harness (AGENTS.md, specs with a definition of done, local and CI tests) matters more than which model you use.
Pointing agents at the Eclipse JDT language server gives exact Java semantics and cuts token use by around 20%, at the cost of one Eclipse backend per agent.
Work rhythm: parallel tasks during the day, specs for big tasks written around 17:00 to run overnight, morning review over coffee; his own review is the bottleneck.
Cache economics: cached input gets a 90% discount, but switching model, editing AGENTS.md, compacting or idling a few minutes busts the cache.
GitHub Advanced Security (CodeQL, Dependabot, secret protection) is part of the agent's feedback loop, not just a human safeguard.
takeaways: Write an AGENTS.md that pins your build tools, test approach and formatting so parallel agents produce consistent code.
Have a second model review complex agent output before you look at it.
Prepare two or three well-specified large tasks at the end of the day and let agents run them overnight.
Turn any process you have done by hand two or three times, such as a release, into a custom skill.
Avoid switching models or editing agent instructions mid-session if you want to keep cached-token discounts.

quotes.text: Most people complain that LLMs are slow. I complain that my laptop is slow.
If you want something better, invest your time in specifications and in testing.

watchIf: You want a measured account of shipping a real Java project with a fleet of coding agents, including the workflow, costs and token-caching details.
